title: Abu Dhabi's Oil Giant Just Found a Way Around the Hormuz Blockade. It Goes Through Oman.
excerpt: ADNOC has resumed naphtha exports by shuttling cargoes from its refinery inside the Gulf to Oman's Sohar port for ship-to-ship transfer — a workaround that could ease Asia's energy crunch.
body:
For 94 days, the Strait of Hormuz has been effectively closed to normal commercial shipping. On Tuesday, a workaround emerged that could begin to ease the pain — and it runs through Oman.

## The Bypass

Abu Dhabi National Oil Company, one of the world's largest oil producers, has resumed exports of naphtha — a key petrochemical feedstock — by deploying a two-stage logistics operation that sidesteps the strait entirely.

The process works like this: tankers carry naphtha from ADNOC's Ruwais refinery, located inside the Gulf, to Oman's Sohar port, which sits outside the Strait of Hormuz on the Arabian Sea coast. At Sohar, the cargoes are transferred ship-to-ship to larger vessels bound for Asia.

Two tankers — the Minerva Pisces and the Torm Gwyneth — loaded naphtha from ADNOC-controlled vessels at Sohar around May 30 and are now heading east, shipping data showed. Traders said more tankers may have followed, though not all vessel movements are visible in tracking data.

ADNOC had halted roughly one million metric tonnes per month of naphtha exports from Ruwais in April after the US-Iran war made transiting the strait untenable for most commercial operators.

## Why Oman Matters

Oman's geography has made it the quiet winner of the Hormuz crisis. Unlike Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Qatar — whose primary export terminals sit inside the Gulf — Oman's coastline runs almost entirely along the Arabian Sea and the Gulf of Oman, placing its ports outside the chokepoint.

This geographic advantage was formally cemented on Monday when the India-Oman Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement came into force, granting India immediate zero-duty access on 98% of Omani tariff lines. The timing is not coincidental. A report by India's Global Trade Research Initiative noted that during the war, India's oil trade actually increased with Oman even as imports from Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the UAE fell by 34%.

"Oman can act as a dependable alternative trade and energy gateway for India when the Strait of Hormuz becomes risky or congested," said GTRI founder Ajay Srivastava.

## The Scale of the Crisis

The ADNOC workaround is resourceful, but it cannot substitute for what has been lost. Before the war began on February 28, approximately 20% of the world's crude oil and refined products — roughly 20 million barrels per day — moved through the Strait of Hormuz. Today, only about 1.2 million barrels per day of crude are reaching Asia through the strait, a drop of more than 90%.

Asia's total seaborne crude arrivals in May were 19.47 million barrels per day, still 22% below the pre-war average. A surge of US crude exports to Asia — hitting a record 2.05 million barrels per day in May — has helped, but comes nowhere close to filling the gap.

The human toll is compounding. Thirty-nine vessel strikes and 11 deaths have been recorded in the region since the war began, according to the International Maritime Organization. Six Maersk container ships remain trapped inside the Gulf. Shipping executives meeting at the Posidonia conference in Athens this week called for "clear rules of engagement" before normal traffic can resume.

## India's Exposure

India imports more than 80% of its crude oil, and the Hormuz closure has forced a rapid reorientation of its supply chains. The country has increased purchases from Latin America, Africa and the US, but at higher freight costs and with longer delivery times.

The Oman route offers a partial solution — particularly for petrochemical feedstocks that Indian refiners need to keep operating. India's largest refiners, including Reliance Industries and Indian Oil Corporation, have been scrambling to secure alternative supplies since March.

The RBI's monetary policy decision on Friday will be shaped in part by the energy picture. Oil at $93 per barrel, combined with heavy foreign portfolio outflows, has kept the rupee under pressure at 95.26 per dollar. The central bank is widely expected to hold rates at 5.25%, but the war's inflationary impact looms over every projection.

## What Comes Next

The ADNOC-Oman workaround is a proof of concept: it demonstrates that Gulf producers can get product to market even with the strait closed, but at higher cost and lower volume. If other producers adopt similar routes, Oman's ports — particularly Sohar and Duqm — could emerge as permanent nodes in a restructured global energy logistics network.

For now, the world waits on Washington and Tehran. Trump said on Tuesday that talks with Iran were ongoing. Iran's Revolutionary Guards reported that 24 vessels had transited the strait in the past 24 hours with Iranian permission. But shipping executives warn that sporadic approvals are not the same as open sea lanes.

Ninety-four days of paralysis have exposed a structural vulnerability in global energy supply chains. The Oman bypass is a patch, not a fix. The fix requires a deal — and that remains elusive.
